content: Pain management following a tonsillectomy is a critical aspect of post-operative care. Local anaesthetics are sometimes administered to the tonsillar region to alleviate pain, but their efficacy in this context has not been rigorously evaluated. The objective of this study was to determine the effectiveness of local anaesthesia, administered either before or after surgery, in reducing post-operative pain after tonsillectomy. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, Medline, Embase, and the Oxford Pain Database. They also reviewed reference lists from relevant publications, including non-English language studies. The most recent search was completed in September 1998. The inclusion criteria for the study were randomized controlled trials involving adults or children undergoing tonsillectomy alone. The interventions studied included local anaesthetic injected into the tonsillar region immediately before tonsil removal, injected after tonsil removal, or applied to the tonsillar region via spray or other methods after tonsil removal. The primary outcomes assessed were the reduction in post-operative analgesic demand, measured by the time elapsed before the first request for analgesia and the total amount of analgesia used. Three reviewers independently extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials. Four authors of the included studies were contacted to clarify details regarding randomization methods or the type of intervention used. Initially, 30 trials were identified, but only six met the inclusion criteria. These six studies were published in English between 1989 and 1997. Trials were excluded for reasons such as the inclusion of additional surgical procedures beyond tonsillectomy, inadequate randomization methods, or insufficient group sizes. Of the six included studies, five involved the injection of local anaesthetic, while one used a local anaesthetic spray. Pain was assessed using validated pain scores and measurements of supplemental analgesic intake. However, some studies also employed inappropriate or potentially post-hoc outcome measures, such as global pain scores, which may have introduced bias. None of the included studies demonstrated a significant difference in pain outcomes between the intervention and control groups, except for certain outcome measures deemed inappropriate, such as the aforementioned global pain scores. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of perioperative local anaesthesia for improving post-operative pain control in patients undergoing tonsillectomy. The trials included in the review were small in size, and many involved the concurrent administration of intravenous opioids during the perioperative period, which may have obscured any potential benefits of the local anaesthetic. The authors emphasized the need for further randomized controlled trials to better evaluate this intervention.
